extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory; legislators, constitutional designers, and informed public interested in representative government
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and practical standards for how representative assemblies should be constituted, what functions they should perform, and how they should interact with executive and administrative organs. Focuses on limits of assemblies, division of labor between deliberation/control and execution, and institutional arrangements to secure good legislation and administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular sovereignty / ultimate control
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole people, or a numerous portion of them, must exercise through deputies the ultimate controlling power; this power must be complete so that the people (via representatives) are masters of the operations of government in the last resort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The constitutional form need not explicitly grant this mastery in every clause; what matters is that the practical distribution of power ensures the popular element's supremacy. If legal provisions or unwritten maxims do not reflect the real preponderance of popular power, they will be changed. Anti-patterns include constitutions whose formal rules concentrate control in organs that lack corresponding popular strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between control and execution
rubrics_metrics.description: A representative assembly's proper role is to control all operations of government in the last resort, not to personally do every part of government business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberation and final sanction are appropriate assembly functions; detailed execution is typically better done by individuals or small bodies with responsibility. Example: a commander who fights in the ranks cannot direct the army effectively. Assemblies that try to do everything risk inefficiency and poor outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assemblies should not administer detailed government functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous representative bodies are ill-suited to administer public departments or to dictate detailed administrative acts; administration requires specialized knowledge and individual responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public administration is a skilled business with many practical rules known to practitioners; assemblies lack the necessary experience and are prone to ignorance, superficiality, and inducement by vested interests. Anti-patterns: assemblies deciding specific administrative acts, leading to jobbery, ill-considered measures, and delayed recognition of harms (since assemblies do not personally bear consequences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiscal role: assemblies vote supplies but do not originate estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: While representative bodies should vote taxes and appropriate revenues, they should not be expected to prepare detailed estimates; money should be granted only on the proposition of the executive (crown/government).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This arrangement places moderation and judgment of detailed application on the executive, which will be held responsible for plans and calculations. The assembly's legitimate power in finance is consent/refusal rather than origination; attempting to originate detailed budgets by the assembly is inefficient and impractical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislation is skilled labor requiring small expert bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Making good laws demands experienced, trained minds and long study; therefore legislative drafting and detailed lawmaking should be entrusted primarily to a small committee or specialized commission rather than a large miscellaneous assembly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proposed permanent Commission of Legislation (or Commission of Codification) would prepare bills, maintain consistency with existing laws, and improve legislation over time. Parliament should retain the power to pass, reject, or remit bills for reconsideration but should not tinker clause-by-clause with expert drafts. Anti-patterns: voting laws clause-by-clause in a large house leading to incoherent, contradictory, or incohesive statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural rule: refer detailed drafting to experts and limit parliamentary amendment
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliament should, where practicable, refer bills (or drafts) to a legislative commission or select committee to be prepared in detail; once framed by experts, Parliament should pass or reject rather than substantially alter the measure itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical devices: use select committees, a standing legislative commission with fixed terms, ability to remit bills back to commission for reconsideration. Avoid amendment in committee of the whole and the habit of tinkering which wastes time and produces incoherent laws. Example anti-pattern: clauses omitted or incongruous ones inserted to conciliate private interests or ill-informed members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assemblies as oversight bodies and forums of opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper office of a representative assembly is to watch and control the government, bring its acts into publicity, compel full exposition and justification of questionable acts, and to act as the nation's Committee of Grievances and Congress of Opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parliament should expose and test opinions publicly, providing a venue where every section and eminent individual can challenge and defend views; such debate is valuable, not mere bavardage. This function enables the government to perceive prevailing opinion and adapt measures accordingly, often without resort to force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointments should be made by responsible individuals, not assemblies
rubrics_metrics.description: The nomination to public employments requires individual responsibility and knowledge of qualifications; assemblies are generally unfit to make appointments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ministers or heads of offices should appoint, bearing personal responsibility for choices. Anti-patterns: appointments made by an assembly for partisan support or jobbery; appointment by committee often favors popularity or vague general ability over specific qualifications, producing misfit appointments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional morality (unwritten conventions) must harmonize with real power
rubrics_metrics.description: Unwritten maxims or positive political morality limit the use of lawful powers and prevent their abuse, but they are only effective if they harmonize with the actual distribution of political strength in society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conventions (e.g., crown assent not used, executive appointed by Commons' majority) survive only while they align with which power is strongest in practice. If constitutional maxims conflict with real preponderance, either laws or conventions will have to change. Example: in Britain, political morality makes the House of Commons the real sovereign despite formal powers of crown and Lords.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding concentration on place-hunting and excessive creation of offices
rubrics_metrics.description: Representative systems are damaged where the populace prizes holding offices (place-hunting) over liberty; excessive multiplication of public employments fosters overgovernment and corruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Healthy representative government discourages multiplication of offices and prefers advancement through business or professions rather than political appointment. Anti-patterns: bureauocracy-ridden nations that multiply offices to increase individual chances of appointment, tolerating higher taxes rather than reducing patronage opportunities.
